claim: Single-particle tracking (SPT) has become an important method to bridge biochemistry and cell biology since it allows direct observation of protein binding and diffusion dynamics in live cells.
source: Single-particle tracking (SPT) has become an important method to bridge biochemistry and cell biology since it allows direct observation of protein binding and diffusion dynamics in live cells.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance and capabilities of SPT, drawing on established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Accurately inferring information from SPT studies is challenging due to biases in both data analysis and experimental design.
source: However, accurately inferring information from SPT studies is challenging due to biases in both data analysis and experimental design.
evidence: This claim is supported by the subsequent detailed discussion of various biases (motion-blur, tracking errors, defocalization) in the manuscript.

claim: Spot-On is an intuitive web-interface that implements a kinetic modeling framework accounting for known biases including molecules moving out-of-focus.
source: To address analysis bias, we introduce 'Spot-On', an intuitive web-interface. Spot-On implements a kinetic modeling framework that accounts for known biases, including molecules moving out-of-focus, and robustly infers diffusion constants and subpopulations from pooled single-molecule trajectories.
evidence: This is a direct description of the tool developed in this study, representing a primary finding.

claim: Stroboscopic photo-activation SPT (spaSPT) minimizes motion-blur bias and tracking errors.
source: To minimize inherent experimental biases, we implement and validate stroboscopic photo-activation SPT (spaSPT), which minimizes motion-blur bias and tracking errors.
evidence: This claim is validated through experimental data presented in Figure 4 showing the effects of different excitation pulse durations.

claim: Spot-On was validated using experimentally realistic simulations and outperforms other methods.
source: We validate Spot-On using experimentally realistic simulations and show that Spot-On outperforms other methods.
evidence: This is supported by the comprehensive simulation results shown in Figure 3 and Table 1 comparing Spot-On to vbSPT and MSDi methods.

claim: Spot-On was applied to spaSPT data from live mammalian cells spanning a wide range of nuclear dynamics.
source: We then apply Spot-On to spaSPT data from live mammalian cells spanning a wide range of nuclear dynamics and demonstrate that Spot-On consistently and robustly infers subpopulation fractions and diffusion constants.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data on H2B-Halo, Halo-CTCF, Halo-Sox2, and Halo-NLS shown in Figure 4.

claim: Recent biological applications of SPT have revealed that transcription factors (TFs) bind mitotic chromosomes.
source: Recent biological applications of SPT have revealed that transcription factors (TFs) bind mitotic chromosomes (Teves et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: SPT has revealed how Polycomb interacts with chromatin.
source: how Polycomb interacts with chromatin (Zhen et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: 'Pioneer factor' TFs bind chromatin dynamically.
source: that 'pioneer factor' TFs bind chromatin dynamically (Swinstead et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: TF binding time correlates with transcriptional activity.
source: that TF binding time correlates with transcriptional activity (Loffreda et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Different nuclear proteins adopt distinct target search mechanisms.
source: that different nuclear proteins adopt distinct target search mechanisms (Izeddin et al., 2014; Rhodes et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: SPT is often seen as less biased and less model-dependent compared to FRAP or FCS.
source: Compared with indirect and bulk techniques such as Fluorescence Recovery After Photobleaching (FRAP) or Fluorescence Correlation Spectroscopy (FCS), SPT is often seen as less biased and less model-dependent (Goulian and Simon, 2000; Mueller et al., 2013; Shen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: SPT makes it possible to directly follow single molecules over time in live cells.
source: In particular, SPT makes it possible to directly follow single molecules over time in live cells and has provided clear evidence that proteins often exist in several subpopulations that can be characterized by their distinct diffusion coefficients (Mueller et al., 2013; Shen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a general statement about SPT capabilities supported by citations.

claim: Nuclear proteins such as TFs and chromatin binding proteins typically show a quasi-immobile chromatin-bound fraction and a freely diffusing fraction inside the nucleus.
source: For example, nuclear proteins such as TFs and chromatin binding proteins typically show a quasi-immobile chromatin-bound fraction and a freely diffusing fraction inside the nucleus.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field about nuclear protein dynamics.

claim: 2D-SPT of proteins freely diffusing inside a 3D nucleus introduces several biases that must be corrected for in order to obtain accurate estimates of subpopulations.
source: However, while SPT of slow-diffusing membrane proteins is an established technology (Weimann et al., 2013), 2D-SPT of proteins freely diffusing inside a 3D nucleus introduces several biases that must be corrected for in order to obtain accurate estimates of subpopulations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the detailed discussion of biases and citations to prior work.

claim: Motion-blur artifact occurs when fast-diffusing molecules move during frame acquisition and spread their emitted photons over multiple pixels.
source: First, while a frame is acquired, fast-diffusing molecules move and spread out their emitted photons over multiple pixels causing a 'motion-blur' artifact (Berglund, 2010; Deschout et al., 2012; Frost et al., 2012; Goulian and Simon, 2000; Izeddin et al., 2014), whereas immobile or slow-diffusing molecules resemble point spread functions (PSFs; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Motion-blur results in under-counting of the fast-diffusing subpopulation.
source: This results in under-counting of the fast-diffusing subpopulation.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the motion-blur phenomenon described.

claim: High particle densities tend to cause tracking errors when localized molecules are connected into trajectories.
source: Second, high particle densities tend to cause tracking errors when localized molecules are connected into trajectories. This can result in incorrect displacement estimates (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 1B and represents established knowledge about tracking challenges.

claim: During 2D SPT of 3D motion, immobile or slow-diffusing molecules remain in-focus until they photobleach and exhibit long trajectories.
source: Third, since SPT generally employs 2D imaging of 3D motion, immobile or slow-diffusing molecules will generally remain in-focus until they photobleach and therefore exhibit long trajectories, whereas fast-diffusing molecules in 3D rapidly move out-of-focus, thus resulting in short trajectories (we refer to this as 'defocalization'; Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 1C and Video 1.

claim: Fast-diffusing molecules in 3D rapidly move out-of-focus during 2D SPT, resulting in short trajectories.
source: whereas fast-diffusing molecules in 3D rapidly move out-of-focus, thus resulting in short trajectories (we refer to this as 'defocalization'; Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 1C and Video 1.

claim: Defocalization results in a time-dependent under-counting of fast-diffusing molecules.
source: This results in a time-dependent under-counting of fast-diffusing molecules (Goulian and Simon, 2000; Kues and Kubitscheck, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Spot-On is available as a web-interface at https://SpotOn.berkeley.edu as well as Python and Matlab packages.
source: Spot-On is available as a web-interface (https://SpotOn.berkeley.edu) as well as Python and Matlab packages.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the availability of the tool.

claim: Spot-On guides users through quality-checks of uploaded datasets consisting of pooled single-molecule trajectories.
source: Spot-On is a user-friendly web-interface that pedagogically guides the user through a series of quality-checks of uploaded datasets consisting of pooled single-molecule trajectories.
evidence: This describes the functionality of the Spot-On tool.

claim: Spot-On performs kinetic model-based analysis that leverages the histogram of molecular displacements over time to infer the fraction and diffusion constant of each subpopulation.
source: It then performs kinetic model-based analysis that leverages the histogram of molecular displacements over time to infer the fraction and diffusion constant of each subpopulation (Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the core analytical approach of Spot-On, illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Spot-On does not directly analyze raw microscopy images.
source: Spot-On does not directly analyze raw microscopy images, since a large number of localization and tracking algorithms exist that convert microscopy images into single-molecule trajectories (for a comparison of particle tracking methods, see (Chenouard et al., 2014); moreover, Spot-On can be one-click interfaced with TrackMate (Tinevez et al., 2017), which allows inspection of trajectories before uploading to Spot-On).
evidence: This describes the input requirements for Spot-On and references existing tracking algorithms.

claim: Spot-On models the distribution of displacements for each subpopulation using Brownian motion under steady-state conditions without state transitions.
source: Spot-On models the distribution of displacements for each subpopulation using Brownian motion under steady-state conditions without state transitions (full model description in Materials and Methods).
evidence: This describes the theoretical model underlying Spot-On.

claim: Spot-On accounts for localization errors that can be either user-defined or inferred from the SPT data.
source: Spot-On also accounts for localization errors (either user-defined or inferred from the SPT data).
evidence: This describes a feature of the Spot-On model.

claim: Spot-On corrects for defocalization bias by explicitly calculating the probability that molecules move out-of-focus as a function of time and their diffusion constant.
source: Crucially, Spot-On corrects for defocalization bias (Figure 1C) by explicitly calculating the probability that molecules move out-of-focus as a function of time and their diffusion constant (Video 1).
evidence: This describes a key feature of Spot-On, illustrated in Video 1.

claim: Spot-On uses the gradual loss of freely diffusing molecules over time as additional information to infer the diffusion constant and size of each subpopulation.
source: In fact, Spot-On uses the gradual loss of freely diffusing molecules over time as additional information to infer the diffusion constant and size of each subpopulation.
evidence: This describes how Spot-On leverages defocalization information.

claim: Spot-On considers either 2 or 3 subpopulations.
source: Spot-On considers either 2 or 3 subpopulations.
evidence: This describes the modeling capabilities of Spot-On.

claim: TFs in nuclei can generally exist in both a chromatin-bound state characterized by slow diffusion and a freely diffusing state associated with rapid diffusion.
source: For instance, TFs in nuclei can generally exist in both a chromatin-bound state characterized by slow diffusion and a freely diffusing state associated with rapid diffusion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about transcription factor dynamics.

claim: Spot-On accurately inferred subpopulation sizes with minimal error in simulations.
source: Spot-On accurately inferred subpopulation sizes with minimal error (Figure 3A–B, Table 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3A-B and Table 1.

claim: Spot-On slightly underestimated the diffusion constant by −4.8% in simulations.
source: but slightly underestimated the diffusion constant (−4.8%; Figure 3B; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3B and Table 1.

claim: The underestimate of diffusion constant by Spot-On was due to particle confinement inside the nucleus.
source: However, this underestimate was due to particle confinement inside the nucleus: Spot-On correctly inferred the diffusion constant when the confinement was relaxed (Figure 3—figure supplement 4; 20 µm nuclear radius instead of 4 µm).
evidence: This claim is supported by additional simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Diffusion constants measured by SPT inside cells should be viewed as apparent diffusion constants.
source: This emphasizes that diffusion constants measured by SPT inside cells should be viewed as apparent diffusion constants.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results showing the effect of confinement.

claim: The MSDi method failed under most conditions regardless of whether all trajectories were used or a fitting filter applied.
source: In contrast, the MSDi method failed under most conditions regardless of whether all trajectories were used (MSDi (all)) or a fitting filter applied (MSDi (R2 >0.8); Figure 3A–B; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results comparing different methods shown in Figure 3A-B and Table 1.

claim: vbSPT performed almost as well as Spot-On for slow-diffusing proteins, but showed larger deviations for fast-diffusing proteins.
source: vbSPT performed almost as well as Spot-On for slow-diffusing proteins, but showed larger deviations for fast-diffusing proteins (Figure 3—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2–3.

claim: 3480 experiments were simulated with parameters spanning the full range of biologically plausible dynamics.
source: We considered the effect of the exposure time (1 ms, 4 ms, 7 ms, 13 ms, 20 ms), the free diffusion constant (from 0.5 µm²/s to 14.5 µm²/s in 0.5 µm²/s increments) and the bound fraction (from 0% to 95% in 5% increments) yielding a total of 3480 different conditions that span the full range of biologically plausible dynamics (Figure 3—figure supplements 2–3; Appendix 1).
evidence: This describes the comprehensive simulation study performed.

claim: Spot-On's ability to infer DFREE and FBOUND was robust to misestimates of the axial detection range of ~100–200 nm.
source: Spot-On's ability to infer DFREE and FBOUND was robust to misestimates of the axial detection range of ~100–200 nm (Figure 3—figure supplement 7)
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7.

claim: Spot-On was minimally affected by the number of timepoints considered and fitting parameters.
source: was minimally affected by the number of timepoints considered and fitting parameters (Figure 3—figure supplements 8–9; see also Appendix 2 for parameter considerations)
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 8–9.

claim: Spot-On inferred the localization error with nanometer precision provided that a significant bound fraction is present.
source: Moreover, Spot-On inferred the localization error with nanometer precision provided that a significant bound fraction is present (Figure 3—figure supplement 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 11.

claim: Just ~3000 short trajectories (mean length ~3–4 frames) were sufficient for Spot-On to reliably infer the underlying dynamics.
source: Finally, we sub-sampled the data sets and found that just ~3000 short trajectories (mean length ~3–4 frames) were sufficient for Spot-On to reliably infer the underlying dynamics (Figure 3—figure supplement 12).
evidence: This claim is supported by jack-knife sampling results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 12.

claim: Spot-On successfully overcomes defocalization and analysis method biases.
source: Taken together, this analysis of simulated SPT data suggests that Spot-On successfully overcomes defocalization and analysis method biases (Figure 1C–D)
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the comprehensive simulation results.

claim: Spot-On accurately and robustly estimates subpopulations and diffusion constants across a wide range of dynamics.
source: accurately and robustly estimates subpopulations and diffusion constants across a wide range of dynamics
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the comprehensive simulation results.

claim: Spot-On outperforms other methods (vbSPT and MSDi).
source: and, finally, outperforms other methods.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the comparative simulation results shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: spaSPT minimizes motion-blurring by using stroboscopic excitation.
source: First, spaSPT minimizes motion-blurring, which is caused by particle movement during the camera exposure time (Figure 1A), by using stroboscopic excitation (Elf et al., 2007; Frost et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the spaSPT method and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PA-JF549 and PA-JF646 dyes in combination with HaloTag labeling made it possible to achieve a signal-to-background ratio greater than 5 with just 1 ms excitation pulses.
source: We found that the bright and photo-stable dyes PA-JF549 and PA-JF646 (Grimm et al., 2016a) in combination with the HaloTag ('Halo') labeling strategy made it possible to achieve a signal-to-background ratio greater than 5 with just 1 ms excitation pulses, thus providing a good compromise between minimal motion-blurring and high signal (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: spaSPT minimizes tracking errors by using photo-activation.
source: Second, spaSPT minimizes tracking errors (Figure 1B) by using photo-activation (Figure 4A) (Grimm et al., 2016a; Manley et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the spaSPT method and is supported by citations and Figure 4A.

claim: Photo-activation allows tracking at extremely low densities (≤1 molecule per nucleus per frame) and thereby minimizes tracking errors.
source: Photo-activation allows tracking at extremely low densities (≤1 molecule per nucleus per frame) and thereby minimizes tracking errors (Izeddin et al., 2014), whilst at the same time generating thousands of trajectories.
evidence: This describes the advantage of photo-activation and is supported by citation.

claim: 1064 spaSPT experiments were performed across 60 different conditions.
source: To generate a large dataset to comprehensively test Spot-On, we performed 1064 spaSPT experiments across 60 different conditions.
evidence: This describes the scale of the experimental validation performed.

claim: Spot-On consistently inferred the diffusion constant across a wide range of frame rates (50 Hz to 200 Hz).
source: Spot-On consistently inferred the diffusion constant (Figure 4G) and total bound fraction across the wide range of frame rates (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental results shown in Figure 4G-H.

claim: All four proteins studied (H2B, CTCF, Sox2, Halo-3xNLS) exhibit apparent anomalous diffusion.
source: This is notable since all four proteins exhibit apparent anomalous diffusion (Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by MSD analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Spot-On is robust to anomalous diffusion despite modeling Brownian motion.
source: and this demonstrates that Spot-On is also robust to anomalous diffusion despite modeling Brownian motion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing consistent parameter estimates despite anomalous diffusion.

claim: The axial detection range was experimentally determined to be ~700 nm.
source: We experimentally determined the axial detection range to be ~700 nm (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is an experimental measurement shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: For fast-diffusing proteins like Halo-3xNLS and H2B-Halo, motion-blurring resulted in a large underestimate of the free diffusion constant.
source: For fast-diffusing proteins like Halo-3xNLS and H2B-Halo, motion-blurring resulted in a large underestimate of the free diffusion constant, whereas the effect on slower proteins like CTCF and Sox2 was minor (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental results shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Motion-blurring caused a ~2 fold overestimate of the bound fraction for rapidly diffusing Halo-3xNLS.
source: Regarding the total bound fraction, motion-blurring caused a ~2 fold overestimate for rapidly diffusing Halo-3xNLS (Figure 4K)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental results shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Motion-blurring had a minor effect on the bound fraction for slower proteins like H2B, CTCF and Sox2.
source: but had a minor effect on slower proteins like H2B, CTCF and Sox2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental results shown in Figure 4K.

claim: JF549 appears to better capture the dynamics of proteins with a minimal bound fraction such as Halo-3xNLS compared to JF646.
source: Similar results were obtained for both dyes for proteins with a significant bound fraction, but we note that JF549 appears to better capture the dynamics of proteins with a minimal bound fraction such as Halo-3xNLS (Figure 4J–K).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental comparison of the two dyes shown in Figure 4J-K.

claim: Using the MTT-algorithm, motion-blurring caused up to a 2-fold error in both the DFREE and FBOUND estimates.
source: Finally, we note that the extent of the bias due to motion-blurring will likely be very sensitive to the localization algorithm. Here, using the MTT-algorithm (Sergé et al., 2008), motion-blurring caused up to a 2-fold error in both the DFREE and FBOUND estimates.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental motion-blur study.

claim: Spot-On can reliably be used even for SPT data collected under constant illumination provided that protein diffusion is sufficiently slow.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that Spot-On can reliably be used even for SPT data collected under constant illumination provided that protein diffusion is sufficiently slow
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the motion-blur experiments.

claim: A clear consensus on how to perform and analyze SPT experiments is currently lacking.
source: However, a clear consensus on how to perform and analyze SPT experiments is currently lacking.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: 2D SPT of fast-diffusing molecules inside 3D cells is subject to a number of inherent experimental and analysis biases.
source: In particular, 2D SPT of fast-diffusing molecules inside 3D cells is subject to a number of inherent experimental (Figure 1A–B) and analysis (Figure 1C–D) biases, which can lead to inaccurate conclusions if not carefully corrected for.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the detailed discussion and figures throughout the manuscript.

claim: Spot-On provides a bias-corrected, comprehensive open-source framework for inferring subpopulations and diffusion constants from pooled SPT data.
source: Spot-On now complements these tools by providing a bias-corrected, comprehensive open-source framework for inferring subpopulations and diffusion constants from pooled SPT data and makes this platform available through a convenient web-interface.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contribution of Spot-On.

claim: The Spot-On platform can easily be extended to other diffusion regimes and models.
source: This platform can easily be extended to other diffusion regimes (Metzler et al., 2014) and models (Lee et al., 2017)
evidence: This is a statement about the extensibility of Spot-On, supported by citations to relevant work.

claim: As 3D SPT methods mature, Spot-On can be extended to 3D SPT data.
source: and, as 3D SPT methods mature, to 3D SPT data.

claim: spaSPT provides an acquisition protocol for tracking fast-diffusing molecules with minimal bias.
source: Moreover, spaSPT provides an acquisition protocol for tracking fast-diffusing molecules with minimal bias.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contribution of spaSPT, supported by the experimental validation.

claim: Spot-On implements and extends a kinetic modeling framework first described in Mazza et al. (2012) and later extended in Hansen et al. (2017).
source: Spot-On implements and extends a kinetic modeling framework first described in Mazza et al. (2012) and later extended in Hansen et al. (2017).

claim: Defocalization is explicitly accounted for in Spot-On by modeling the fraction of particles that remain in focus over time as a function of their diffusion constant.
source: Defocalization is explicitly accounted for by modeling modeling the fraction of particles that remain in focus over time as a function of their diffusion constant.

claim: Uncorrected defocalization results in a 4-fold undercounting of freely-diffusing molecules.

claim: Spot-On allows the user to choose between PDF- and CDF-fitting of the kinetic model to the empirical displacement distributions.
source: Spot-On allows the user to choose between PDF- and CDF-fitting of the kinetic model to the empirical displacement distributions; CDF-fitting is generally most accurate for smaller datasets and the two are similar for large datasets (Figure 3—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This describes a feature of Spot-On and is supported by comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 9.

claim: CDF-fitting is generally most accurate for smaller datasets.
source: CDF-fitting is generally most accurate for smaller datasets and the two are similar for large datasets (Figure 3—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of PDF and CDF fitting shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 9.

claim: The kinetic model assumes diffusion to be ideal Brownian motion, even though most proteins inside a cell show some degree of anomalous diffusion.
source: First, the kinetic model assumes diffusion to be ideal Brownian motion, even though it is widely acknowledged that the motion of most proteins inside a cell shows some degree of anomalous diffusion.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the Spot-On model.

claim: Spot-On models the localization error as the static mean localization error.
source: Second, Spot-On models the localization error as the static mean localization error and this feature can be used to infer the actual localization error from the data.
